newsitem.title: USA: U.S. utilities may burn plutonium from bombs - paper.
newsitem.headline: U.S. utilities may burn plutonium from bombs - paper.

text.p: Two U.S. utilities may join with European nuclear plants in a project to burn plutonium harvested from surplus nuclear weapons in their nuclear generating plants, a newspaper reported on Saturday.

Northern Illinois' Unicom Corp. and North Carolina's Duke Power Co., which have the most nuclear plants among U.S. utilities, would join with the European facilities to form Project PEACE (Plutonium Excess Arms Converted to Electricity), the Chicago Sun-Times reported.
The newspaper, citing a report in the authoritative trade journal Energy Daily, called the plan the ultimate in "beating swords into ploughshares."

A proposed test burn of plutonium would take place as early as 1999 as part of a two-pronged approach to deal with about 50 tonnes of highly radioactive plutonium taken from thousands of dismantled nuclear weapons. The surplus weapons would come from the U.S. and former Soviet Union stockpiles.
The other disposal plan calls for weapons-grade plutonium to be encased with radioactive waste in glass logs and buried, the Sun-Times' report said.
Some European reactors already use a fuel made from a combination of weapons-grade plutonium and uranium, but a U.S. plant to produce the mixture was years away, the report said.

The report also raised safety issues that could affect the plan, such as the possibility of transporting plutonium over long distances, making it vulnerable to a hijacking, and the question of disposing of the fuel that remains highly radioactive even after it is spent. It also questioned whether government subsidies provided to the utilities would provide an unfair competitive advantage to controversial nuclear power over other sources of electricity generation.

In addition, three of the six nuclear power plants operated by Unicom's Commonwealth Edison unit were on the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's "watch list" for various operating and maintenance shortcomings.
Commonwealth Edison could not be reached for comment.
